title: Part 1
text: Two wide, unblinking eyes stare out of a shocked fish face in a Helsinki museum. The real story behind it is stranger than the joke.

title: Part 2
text: That fish is Sacabambaspis, and the face is a museum model in the Finnish Museum of Natural History.
nxt: In August 2022, a photo of it spread on Twitter, mostly as a joke about a badly made reconstruction.

title: Part 3
text: But the animal was real. Sacabambaspis was a jawless fish that lived in Ordovician seas, roughly 450 million years ago, long before the first dinosaur.
nxt: Its fossils come from the Anzaldo Formation near Cochabamba in Bolivia.

nxt: The name combines the nearby village of Sacabamba with the Greek word aspis, meaning shield. The species name honors the French paleontologist Philippe Janvier.

title: Part 4
text: It was small. An adult was about twenty-five centimeters long, roughly the length of a shoe. Its front half was covered by bony armor.
nxt: One large shield covered the back of the head and body, and another covered the belly. Behind that armor trailed a flexible tail covered in small scales.

title: Part 5
text: Now the eyes. In most modern fish, the eyes sit on the sides of the head, which gives a wide view for spotting predators.
nxt: Sacabambaspis had its eyes set toward the front of the head. So the meme got that part at least partly right.

title: Part 6
text: What about the shocked mouth? That is the part to be careful with.
nxt: Reconstructing a fish from flattened, broken fossils is hard, and a sculptor has to guess what the soft parts looked like.

title: Part 7
text: So when you see that famous face, remember two things. The fish was real, and the look on its face was partly a guess. The goofy face was never the whole story.
